canonical_topic: Spent fuel and nuclear waste handling
definition: After use, reactor fuel, control rods, and cooling water remain radioactive (still undergoing fission, just much more slowly), and used fuel may be reprocessed to recover unused U-235 before the remaining waste must be disposed of.
core_idea: Toxic/radioactive waste can either be diluted across a wide area or concentrated into a smaller volume; because most jurisdictions restrict release of toxic substances into the environment, dilution is generally not viable, so nuclear waste ends up concentrated and stored in dedicated facilities.
key_points: Spent fuel, control rods, and cooling water are all radioactive after reactor use, continuing fission at a much slower rate.
Used fuel may be reprocessed to remove remaining usable U-235.
Toxic waste in general has two disposal strategies: dilute over a wide area, or concentrate into a smaller, more toxic volume.
Regulatory limits on releasing toxic substances into the biosphere generally rule out dilution as a viable approach.
As a result, nuclear waste is concentrated and placed in storage facilities intended to be far from populated areas.
relationships: This waste-concentration outcome connects directly to the later point that concentrated nuclear waste is a distinct, immediate health hazard compared to diffuse fossil-fuel pollution.
caveats: Diluting nuclear waste is not treated as a real regulatory option — the author frames concentration/storage as effectively the only path given release limits.
